bib.title: Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Least-to-Most Prompting Enables Complex Reasoning in Large Language Models", Denny Zhou, Nathanael Schärli, Le Hou, Jason Wei, Nathan Scales, Xuezhi Wang, Dale Schuurmans, Claire Cui, Olivier Bousquet, Quoc Le, Ed Chi (Google Research, Brain Team). ICLR 2023 conference paper, arXiv 2205.10625v3 (16 Apr 2023).

COVERAGE: I read all 202,907 characters, 61 pages. The main text (pp.1-9), every results table, every error analysis, the prompt contexts and the GSM8K appendix (pp.56-61) were read line by line. I skimmed the long worked-example outputs: SCAN success and failure transcripts (pp.33-45) and the DROP football prompt bodies and cases 2-3 (pp.49-53). I checked them for prose or numbers and found only the transcripts and the one-line "Analysis" notes. The figures script found one caption (Fig. 1, p.2).

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: On SCAN length split, least-to-most (L2M) with code-davinci-002 reaches 99.7%. Chain-of-thought (CoT) gets 16.2% and standard prompting 16.7%.
  number: 99.7 vs 16.2 vs 16.7
  setup: GPT-3 code-davinci-002. The decomposition prompt has 8 exemplars and the mapping prompt 14. Python-expression intermediate output is expanded by a script. CoT uses the same 14-exemplar mapping prompt without decomposition.
  quote: "code-davinci-002 16.7 16.2 99.7" (Table 8); "Using code-davinci-002, least-to-most prompting achieves an accuracy of 99.7% under length split."
  where: p.6, Table 8
- claim: The SCAN result holds on every split and on the full dataset. Specialised neural-symbolic models train on more than 15,000 examples for comparison.
  number: >=99%, 14 exemplars, >15,000
  setup: code-davinci-002
  quote: "it can solve the compositional generalization benchmark SCAN in any split (including length split) with an accuracy of at least 99% using just 14 exemplars, compared to only 16% accuracy with chain-of-thought prompting"; "trained on the entire training set containing over 15,000 examples"
  where: p.1 abstract; p.6 "We find that its solving rate remains the same"
- claim: SCAN results by model. text-davinci-002 gets 76.0 with L2M and 0.0 with CoT. code-davinci-001 gets 60.7 with L2M and 0.0 with CoT.
  number: 76.0 / 0.0; 60.7 / 0.0
  setup: text-davinci-002 was scored on a random 100 commands
  quote: "text-davinci-002 6.0 0.0 76.0"; "code-davinci-001 0.4 0.0 60.7"; "The results of text-davinci-002 are based on a random subset of 100 commands."
  where: p.6 Table 8
- claim: On last-letter concatenation, L2M degrades far more slowly with list length than CoT. Both use 2 exemplars of lists of length 2-3. Standard prompting scores 0.
  number: L=4/6/8/10/12. CoT 84.2/69.2/50.2/39.8/31.8. L2M 94.0/88.4/83.0/76.4/74.0.
  setup: code-davinci-002. 500 lists per length, words sampled from a Wiktionary top-10k list.
  quote: "Chain-of-Thought 84.2 69.2 50.2 39.8 31.8 / Least-to-Most 94.0 88.4 83.0 76.4 74.0"
  where: p.4 Table 4
- claim: Adding exemplars to CoT does not close the gap. 8-shot CoT (573 tokens) still trails 2-shot L2M (123 tokens) at L=12.
  number: 38.4% vs 74.0%; 37.4% with 4-shot CoT; 76.6% with 4-shot L2M
  setup: code-davinci-002
  quote: "even if we compare 2-shot least-to-most (prompt size 123 GPT3 tokens) to 8-shot chain-of-thought (prompt size 573 GPT3 tokens) ... for L = 12, we have least-to-most at 74.0% vs. chain-of-thought at 38.4%"; "4 code-002 96.0 92.0 84.6 80.2 76.6"
  where: p.16-17, Table 13
- claim: Model generation matters a great deal. code-davinci-001 nearly fails with either method.
  number: L2M at L=4 is 19.6% on code-davinci-001 vs 96% on code-davinci-002. text-davinci-002 L2M gets 66.0 at L=12.
  quote: "Even for the shortest list size (L = 4), the accuracy for least-to-most prompting is only 19.6% compared to 96% for code-davinci-002."
  where: p.17
- claim: On GSM8K, L2M barely beats CoT overall. Its gain sits in problems needing 5 or more steps, and it is slightly worse on 2-step problems. Both prompts use one 2-step exemplar, and L2M's decomposition and solving are merged into a single pass.
  number: overall 62.39 vs 60.87. 2 steps 74.53 vs 76.68. >=5 steps 45.23 vs 39.07 (+15.77% relative).
  setup: code-davinci-002, 1-shot
  quote: "Overall, least-to-most prompting only slightly improves chain-of-thought prompting: from 60.97% to 62.39%. However, least-to-most prompting essentially improves chain-of-thought prompting in solving problems which need at least 5 steps to be solved: from 39.07% to 45.23%"; Table 12 "Least-to-Most 62.39 74.53 68.91 59.73 45.23 / Chain-of-Thought 60.87 76.68 67.29 59.39 39.07"
  where: p.7-8 Tables 11-12; Table 18 p.56
- claim: Where it does not help: with engineered multi-exemplar GSM8K prompts, L2M is no better than CoT, and in fact slightly lower.
  number: CoT (best, 4 ex) 68.61 vs L2M (best, 7 decomposition + 4 solving ex) 68.01. Original 8-shot CoT 61.18.
  quote: "We do not observe improvement in overall accuracy from least-to-most prompting compared to chain-of-thought prompting in this setting, where most of the test questions do not require more steps more steps to solve than the demonstration examples."; "Chain-of-Thought (best) 68.613 / Least-to-Most (best) 68.01"
  where: p.57 Table 19
- claim: On DROP numerical subsets, L2M beats CoT by a wide margin. The authors attribute this to trivial decomposability.
  number: code-davinci-002 non-football 82.45 vs 74.77; football 73.42 vs 59.56
  setup: 5-exemplar (non-football) or 6-exemplar (football) decomposition prompt plus a 3-exemplar solving prompt; CoT uses 3 exemplars
  quote: "Least-to-Most 82.45 73.42 62.39"; "That is probably because most problems in DROP can be trivially decomposed."
  where: p.7 Table 11
- claim: The DROP gain replicates on other models.
  number: text-davinci-002 74.20/63.40 vs CoT 60.80/57.40 (500 cases each). LM-540B 79.24/69.98 vs CoT 63.84/67.35 (3988/1862 cases).
  quote: "Least-to-Most 74.20 63.40"; "Least-to-Most 79.24 69.98"
  where: p.46-47 Tables 16-17
- claim: Most GSM8K failures are decomposition failures. Given a hand-written decomposition, almost every failed problem gets solved (qualitative, no count given).
  number: none
  quote: "almost every problem in GSM8K that least-to-most prompting fails to solve can be eventually solved by using a manually crafted decomposition"
  where: p.7
- claim: DROP L2M error breakdown from 20 random failures.
  number: 4 decomposition, 13 subproblem-solving, 3 wrong labels
  quote: "4 are due to wrong problem decomposition"; "13 are due to wrong problem solving"; "3 are due to wrong “ground truth”"
  where: p.54-55
- claim: The remaining errors are execution slips, not decomposition errors. SCAN has 13 total failures: 6 on twice/thrice after "around", 7 reading "after" as "and". Last-letter failures are mostly concatenation errors.
  number: 13 SCAN failures; e.g. 13 and 19 concatenation errors among 20 sampled failures (2-shot, L=4 and L=12)
  quote: "there are 13 failures in total from least-to-most prompting: 6 of them incorrectly interpret “twice” and “thrice” following “around”, and the rest incorrectly interpret “after” as “and”"
  where: p.6; Table 14 p.17; Table 15 p.32
- claim: The decomposition step alone is easy for list tasks.
  number: 100% up to length 12
  setup: text-davinci-002, 2 exemplars
  quote: "The following prompt context achieves 100% accuracy on this task when using the text-davinci-002 model."
  where: p.14
- claim: The Python-expression expansion can itself be done by prompting.
  number: 99.7% on 1000 expressions; 6 exemplars
  quote: "we present a prompt that achieves 99.7% accuracy on a random sample of 1000 Python expressions"
  where: p.45

TWO-STAGE FORMAT (p.2-3): "1. Decomposition. The prompt in this stage contains constant examples that demonstrate the decomposition, followed by the specific question to be decomposed. 2. Subproblem solving. The prompt in this stage consists of three parts: (1) constant examples demonstrating how subproblems are solved; (2) a potentially empty list of previously answered subquestions and generated solutions, and (3) the question to be answered next." The original problem is appended as the final subproblem, and each answer is appended to the prompt before the next subquestion. The paper adds: "Least-to-most prompting can be combined with other prompting techniques like chain-of-thought ... and self-consistency ... but does not need to be. Also, for some tasks, the two stages ... can be merged to form a single-pass prompt." The key contrast with CoT is that L2M exemplars "illustrate a base case and a recursive step" and build on earlier answers, whereas CoT exemplars "are independent of each other" (Tables 2-3, p.3-4).

LIMITS:
- Authors concede (Sec 5, p.9): "Decomposition prompts typically don't generalize well across different domains". A math decomposition prompt does not work on StrategyQA-style questions ("Did Aristotle use a laptop?").
- Authors also concede: "Generalizing decomposition can even be difficult within the same domain". They say the strong results come "because decomposition in these tasks is relatively straightforward."
- Gains over CoT are small or absent when test problems are no harder than the exemplars (GSM8K engineered prompts, 2-step problems).
- SCAN relies on Python-notation intermediates plus a postprocessing script, which is partly backed by the 99.7% prompted expansion.
- No variance or seeds are reported. text-davinci-002 results use 100-example subsets.
- Dated: every model is a deprecated GPT-3 or Codex variant (code-davinci-001/002, text-davinci-002), plus an unnamed "LM-540B". Prompts were sized for a 2048-token limit. Some multi-call cost is unreported, beyond the token counts for the last-letter task.
- Sec 6 frames prompting as "unidirectional" and argues for bidirectional interaction.

BUILDS ON: chain-of-thought (Wei et al., 2022; Chowdhery et al., 2022); natural language rationales (Ling et al., 2017; Cobbe et al., 2021); few-shot prompting (Brown et al., 2020); self-consistency (Wang et al., 2022b). The name comes from educational psychology (Libby et al., 2008). Benchmarks: SCAN (Lake & Baroni, 2018), last-letter concatenation (Wei et al., 2022), GSM8K (Cobbe et al., 2021), DROP (Dua et al., 2019). Related decomposition and chaining work: Perez et al. (2020) on independent single-hop subquestions; Wang et al. (2022a) on iterative prompting; Yang et al. (2022) SeqZero; Wu et al. (2022) AI Chains. The paper says it "chains the processes of problem decomposition and subproblem solving." It contrasts its dependent, ordered subquestions with Perez's independent ones.

CODE (prompts, verbatim):
- Last-letter L2M solving exemplars, Table 2 p.3: Q: “think, machine” A: The last letter of “think” is “k”. The last letter of “machine” is “e”. Concatenating “k”, “e” leads to “ke”. So, “think, machine” outputs “ke”. / Q: “think, machine, learning” A: “think, machine” outputs “ke”. The last letter of “learning” is “g”. Concatenating “ke”, “g” leads to “keg”. So, “think, machine, learning” outputs “keg”.
- GSM8K single-pass L2M exemplar, Table 9 p.7: A: Let’s break down this problem: 1. How many apples does Anna have? 2. How many apples do they have together? / 1. Anna has 2 more apples than Elsa. So Anna has 2 + 5 = 7 apples. / 2. Elsa and Anna have 5 + 7 = 12 apples together. / The answer is: 12.
- Decomposition template, p.59: A: To answer the question “How old is Kody?”, we need to know: “How old is Mohamed?”, “How old was Mohamed four years ago?”, “How old was Kody four years ago?”.
- Mechanics of the 1-shot L2M on p.58: the prompt ends "Let’s break down this problem:". The model's reply is appended, followed by "The answer is:", as a second request.

FIGURES:
- Fig. 1, p.2: "Least-to-most prompting solving a math word problem in two stages: (1) query the language model to decompose the problem into subproblems; (2) query the language model to sequentially solve the subproblems." It shows the two-call pipeline and the answer being fed forward in a single picture, which suits a chaining or decomposition note.
- Table 4 (p.4) or Table 13 (p.17) is not a figure but would plot well as accuracy against list length for CoT vs L2M. Table 12 (p.8) does the same by GSM8K step count.

PROBLEMS:
- The GSM8K CoT number is inconsistent within the paper: the text says "60.97%", Table 11 and Table 12 say 60.87, and Table 19 says 60.88 (p.7, 8, 57). Cite the table value (60.87).
- Appendix 8.2 prose calls "text-davinci-002" the "best model" and mentions "text-davinci-001". Table 15's columns are code-002 / code-001 / text-002, so the prose appears to mix up model names (p.32).
- There are broken cross-references ("Table ??", p.14, 16, 46).
- Appendix 10.1 points to post-processing "described in Section 3.3 for DROP", which Section 3.3 does not describe.
- Earlier preprint versions had prompt errors. The corrected Standard and CoT (best) GSM8K figures differ from those versions (footnote 3, p.57: earlier 18.65 and 62.77).
- Table 18's "Accuracy change" row is a relative change, (aL/aC)−1, not percentage points.
- No embedded instructions in the text. Extraction quality was good, apart from ligatures and spaced small-caps headings.
